correctness.rationale: For every binary cut, each edge initially crossing the cut keeps its sign under I+epsilon Q with 0<epsilon<1/2, and equal-labelled edges contribute epsilon times the absolute directional difference. Thus J((I+epsilon Q)1_S)=J(1_S)+epsilon Phi(S) exactly. The two left-label cases produce respectively Phi=(s/q)W-(1+2s/q)C(Y) and Phi=|d|B-(1+d)A+sum_{j in Y}tau_j(s). All other cuts are complements. Column singleton inequalities control all right-only cuts by a sharp sum bound; maximizing fixed-cardinality mixed cuts selects the largest scores. Coarea and iterated Euler contractions imply semigroup contraction for all real signals and all t; a positive cut derivative gives small-time failure. Exact-rational checker executes separate tests 25,728 cuts in 276 positive profiles and 12,576 Euler inequalities. Finite testing is corroboration, not proof.

originality.rationale: Actual mathematical-index searches and accessible prior statements did not identify a theorem implying the \(q\ge3\) arbitrary-weight, degree-normalized heat-semigroup sorted-cut classification. The most relevant primary texts develop graph TV/coarea and separate heat gradient estimates without this particular weighted contraction cone. Existing tree and cycle classifications apply to \(q\le2\), not the new \(q\ge3\) mixed-cut obstruction; unweighted multipartite classifications leave arbitrary anisotropic variation weights and normalized rates unresolved. This is a best-knowledge finding, not a proof of global uniqueness.

value.rationale: The complete bipartite \(K_{2,q}\) is a natural family interpolating a three-vertex path (\(q=1\)), a cycle (\(q=2\)), and a multicycle graph (\(q\ge3\)). The theorem gives an exact constructive admissibility cone for arbitrary positive edge-variation weights and fixed normalized jump rates; its \(O(q^2\log q)\) test replaces \(2^{q+2}\) possible binary cuts. A strictly positive five-vertex weight configuration passes all singleton tests but fails a mixed-cut test, proving the first genuinely nonlocal weight constraint appears at \(q=3\). This is a structural and computationally useful classification rather than a renamed norm bound or unmotivated numerical slice.
